302.title: Nuns in the Theravada
302.hook: the nuns' order died out in Theravada lands; some now revive it and some do not; both views are held in good faith
302.howItsDone: In Sri Lanka some women are now fully ordained as bhikkhunis, while in Thailand, Myanmar and Sri Lanka many women live as precept-keeping renunciants (mae chi, thilashin, dasa sil mata) in white or pink robes; the main monastic bodies of Thailand and Myanmar do not recognize bhikkhuni ordination.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: ordaining for a while, and your line, for a while. Did you set one small thing down for a day, and notice the space it left? Day three hundred two.
screen: `ORDAINING FOR A WHILE — FOR A WHILE.`

segments.voice: Walk into a temple in Thailand early in the morning and you may see a woman with a shaved head, dressed in white, sweeping the courtyard before the monks come back from the alms round. She keeps eight precepts. She meditates for hours. She may have lived this way for forty years. But she isn't a nun in the full sense the old texts describe, and in most of the Theravada world, she can't become one. Why not? Today's answer is a real disagreement, and both sides care about it deeply.
screen: `A WOMAN IN WHITE, SWEEPING AT DAWN.` → `EIGHT PRECEPTS, FORTY YEARS.` → `WHY NOT A FULL NUN?`

segments.voice: Start at the beginning. The Vinaya tells how Mahapajapati, the aunt who raised the Buddha, asked to go forth. With Ananda speaking for her, the Buddha agreed, and the order of bhikkhunis, fully ordained nuns, began. Their voices survive: the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, is among the oldest collections of religious poems by women anywhere. For centuries the nuns' order flourished in Sri Lanka, and tradition says Sri Lankan nuns helped give ordination to women in China in the fifth century. Then, around the eleventh century, in a time of war and famine, the order in Sri Lanka died out. There's no clear record of it continuing anywhere else in the Theravada lands. Here is the knot. The Vinaya says a woman's full ordination is given by both nuns and monks together. With no Theravada nuns left, many elders conclude it can no longer be given: the rule needs nuns, and there are none. They are guarding the code exactly as it was handed down. Others point to the nuns of East Asia, whose lineage traces back, in part, to those Sri Lankan women. Since the late 1990s, women have been fully ordained with their help, and today hundreds of bhikkhunis live in Sri Lanka, with smaller communities elsewhere. They are guarding what the Buddha himself began. In Thailand and Myanmar the main monastic bodies don't recognize these ordinations. Meanwhile, many women keep eight or ten precepts in white or pink robes, honored, practicing, teaching. Both views are held in good faith, by people who love the same teaching. The question is still open.
screen: `MAHAPAJAPATI ASKS TO GO FORTH.` · `THE ORDER FADES IN SRI LANKA.` · `THE RULE NEEDS NUNS TO ORDAIN NUNS.` · `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH IN GOOD FAITH.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION IS STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: For this sit, honor one woman who practiced. It could be Mahapajapati, who asked first. It could be Kisa Gotami, whom you met with the mustard seed. It could be a grandmother, a teacher, or the woman in white sweeping the courtyard. Hold her in mind. On each out-breath, if you like, silently wish her well: may she be at ease. Then let her go, and simply sit. The bell holds the time.
Nuns in the Theravada. The order began with Mahapajapati, faded in Sri Lanka a thousand years ago, and is being revived by some and not by others.
screen: `NUNS IN THE THERAVADA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the question is still open. Today, when you meet a disagreement, try saying both sides fairly before you say which one you lean toward. Day three hundred two.

303.title: The Path of Purification
303.hook: Buddhaghosa's fifth-century manual: virtue, concentration, wisdom
303.howItsDone: Theravada monks and meditation teachers study the Visuddhimagga as the classic guide to the path, and many meditation centers organize their teaching around its three trainings of virtue, concentration and wisdom.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: nuns in the Theravada, and your line, the question is still open. Did you manage to say both sides of something fairly? Day three hundred three.
screen: `NUNS IN THE THERAVADA — THE QUESTION IS STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: Imagine a job interview where they hand you two lines of poetry and say: show us what you understand. That's the story told about a scholar named Buddhaghosa. Sometime in the fifth century he came from India to Sri Lanka, to the Great Monastery at Anuradhapura, hoping to work on the old commentaries kept there. The elders weren't going to hand their library to a stranger. So they gave him a verse and waited. He went away and came back with a book. Today: that book, the Path of Purification.
screen: `TWO LINES AND A TEST.` → `THE GREAT MONASTERY, SRI LANKA.` → `HE CAME BACK WITH A BOOK.`

segments.voice: The verse comes from a short sutta. A deity asks the Buddha: there's a tangle inside and a tangle outside, and people are caught in it; who can untangle this tangle? The Buddha answers, in paraphrase: a wise person, grounded in virtue, who develops the mind and understanding, ardent and discerning, can untangle it. Buddhaghosa built his whole book on that answer. In Pali it's the Visuddhimagga, visuddhi, purification, and magga, path. Its three parts are the three trainings you can already name. First, sila, virtue: the precepts, the monk's rules, guarding the senses, living simply. Virtue steadies the ground. Second, samadhi, concentration, or calm: forty subjects for meditation, from the breath to the immeasurables to a simple colored disc, matched to a person's temperament, so a restless mind and a heavy mind get different medicine. Calm clears the water. Third, panna, wisdom: seeing the heaps, the chain of causes, and the stages of insight you met in noting, until change, unease and not-self are seen directly. Wisdom sees what the clear water shows. The Sri Lankan chronicle adds a story people still tell: the gods hid the finished manuscript twice, Buddhaghosa wrote it out three times, and when the elders laid the three copies side by side, they matched word for word. Whatever you make of that, the elders gave him the library. For fifteen centuries this book has been the Theravada teacher's map, and the modern Burmese insight methods still lean on it. Three trainings, in order. Virtue, calm, wisdom.
screen: `THE TANGLE INSIDE AND OUTSIDE.` · `SILA — VIRTUE STEADIES.` · `SAMADHI — CALM CLEARS.` · `PANNA — WISDOM SEES.` · then, large: `VIRTUE, CALM, WISDOM.`

segments.voice: For this sit, walk the three trainings once. Start with virtue: recall one precept you kept today, even a small one, like a kind word where a sharp one was ready. Then calm: let the breath lengthen, and let the mind settle on it, like silt sinking in a glass. Then wisdom: notice one thing changing right now, a sound, a sensation, a thought. Name them softly as you go: virtue, calm, wisdom. The bell holds the time.
Visuddhimagga. The Path of Purification, Buddhaghosa's fifth-century map of the whole path in three trainings.
screen: `VISUDDHIMAGGA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: virtue, calm, wisdom. Today, when something knots you up, ask which of the three would loosen it: a better action, a quieter mind, or a clearer look. Day three hundred three.

what it means: a map of the whole path in three trainings: virtue, calm and wisdom.

what a scholar hears: Buddhaghosa worked from the Sinhala commentaries of the Mahavihara, and the book's forty meditation subjects and stages of insight shaped Theravada teaching for fifteen centuries.

304.title: A Theravada day
304.hook: chanting, the alms round, sitting, walking, sharing merit
304.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the day usually runs from pre-dawn chanting to the alms round, a meal before noon, sitting and walking meditation, chores and evening chanting; lay people offer food and often pour water while the monks chant, sharing the merit with the dead and all beings.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Visuddhimagga, and your line, virtue, calm, wisdom. When something knotted you up, which of the three loosened it? Day three hundred four, the last day with the elders.
screen: `VISUDDHIMAGGA — VIRTUE, CALM, WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Four in the morning, in a forest monastery in northeast Thailand. It's dark. A wooden bell is struck, slowly, then faster. Somewhere a gecko answers. Monks come down the paths from their huts with flashlights, and the hall fills with the sound of Pali chanting. By the time the sky turns gray, they're walking barefoot into the village with their bowls. For two weeks we've looked at the way of the elders from the outside. Today: one whole day from the inside, and what its shape is for.
screen: `4 A.M. — A WOODEN BELL.` → `CHANTING IN THE DARK.` → `BAREFOOT AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: The day opens with chanting. Homage first, the line you learned in the practices camp, "Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa": homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened. Then the refuges, and verses on the qualities of the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Then the alms round, the pindapata. The monks walk in a line, eyes down, and people wait by the road with rice. Nobody asks. Nobody haggles. Food goes into the bowl, the giver often bows, and the monk moves on. Back at the monastery comes the meal, taken before noon, and then the long middle of the day: sitting, walking meditation on a cleared lane, sweeping leaves, sewing, study, a talk from the teacher. In the evening, more chanting. And threaded through it is the sharing of merit. When lay people offer food, the monks chant a blessing, and the givers slowly pour water from a small vessel into a bowl, letting the good of the gift flow out to their dead and to all beings. Why this shape? Because each part trains the others. Chanting sets the mind. The alms round keeps monks humble and villagers generous. Sitting and walking turn calm into seeing. Sharing keeps the good from becoming a private bank account. Now look back at two weeks with the elders: the way of the elders. Three baskets. The forest remembers. Rules as a shelter. Two wings. See clearly. Rising, falling. A map, not a scoreboard. Entering the stream. Give and receive. For a while. The question is still open. Virtue, calm, wisdom. And today, the elders' day.
screen: `CHANTING AT DAWN.` · `THE ALMS ROUND.` · `SITTING, WALKING, SWEEPING.` · `SHARING THE MERIT.` · then, large: `THE ELDERS' DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the day in miniature. If you like, bow once toward whatever you use as a shrine, or just toward the room. Take three slow steps, feeling each foot lift and land. Then sit, and let the breath be your whole task. When the bell ends the sit, try the last piece: silently let whatever good came from it go out to someone who has died, and then to everyone. Another day, you can stretch this shape to fifteen minutes. The bell holds the time.
A Theravada day. Chanting, the alms round, sitting and walking, and sharing the merit: a shape in which each part trains the others.
screen: `A THERAVADA DAY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the elders' day. Today, give your own day one piece of that shape: a quiet start, a meal eaten with attention, or a moment at night sharing the good. Day three hundred four.

screen: `DAY 304 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ROOF OF THE WORLD.`

305.title: The roof of the world
305.hook: Buddhism reached Tibet from the seventh century; its path is called the diamond vehicle
305.howItsDone: Vajrayana Buddhism is practiced in Tibet, Bhutan, Mongolia, the Himalayan regions of Nepal and India, and in Tibetan communities worldwide; practitioners combine Mahayana teaching with mantra, visualization and ritual under the guidance of a teacher.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Theravada day, and your line, the elders' day. Did your own day get a quiet start, an attentive meal, or a moment of sharing? Day three hundred five, and a new two weeks.
screen: `A THERAVADA DAY — THE ELDERS' DAY.`

segments.voice: Picture the highest plateau on earth. Much of it sits higher than the top of most mountains in Europe. The air is thin, the light is hard, and the wind never quite stops. Barley grows, yaks graze, and the winters are long. Up here, over more than a thousand years, a whole civilization organized itself around the Buddha's teaching: monasteries the size of towns, chants that rumble in the chest, colors everywhere. For two weeks we walked with the elders. Now we climb. Today: the roof of the world, and the name of its path.
screen: `THE HIGHEST PLATEAU ON EARTH.` → `THIN AIR, HARD LIGHT, WIND.` → `A PATH BUILT UP HERE.`

segments.voice: Buddhism reached Tibet in waves. Tibetan tradition says the seventh-century king Songtsen Gampo married princesses from Nepal and China, and each brought an image of the Buddha to Lhasa. A century later, King Trisong Detsen invited two teachers from India: the scholar Shantarakshita and the master Padmasambhava, whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche, the precious teacher. Stories say Padmasambhava tamed the spirits of the land, and together they founded Samye, Tibet's first monastery. More teachers came over the next centuries, carrying texts across the Himalayas to be translated with great care. The path they built is called the Vajrayana. Yana means vehicle. Vajra is harder to pin down, and that's the point. In old India it was the thunderbolt of the god Indra. In Buddhism it became the diamond: nothing can break it, and it cuts through everything. Tibetans call it dorje, and in rituals a teacher holds a small metal dorje in the right hand and a bell in the left: method and wisdom, together. The diamond vehicle keeps the Mahayana heart, the wish to wake up for all beings, and adds its own tools: mantras, visualizations, rituals, and a close bond with a teacher. You'll meet each of them over these two weeks. Today it's practiced in Tibet and among Tibetans in exile, and in Bhutan, Mongolia, the Himalayan regions of Nepal and India, and beyond. As with the elders, we'll learn this path on its own terms, beside the others, never above or below them. The diamond vehicle.
screen: `KINGS, PRINCESSES, AN IMAGE IN LHASA.` · `GURU RINPOCHE AND SAMYE.` · `VAJRA: THUNDERBOLT, THEN DIAMOND.` · `DORJE AND BELL — METHOD AND WISDOM.` · then, large: `THE DIAMOND VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: For this sit, picture the high plateau. Imagine the air thin and cold on your face, and the sky a deep, almost dark blue. Far off, a white monastery on a ridge. Let the breath be slow, as it would be at that height, where nobody hurries up a hill. Feel how big the space is, and how small and steady your breath is inside it. When the mind wanders, come back to the wide sky. The bell holds the time.
Vajrayana. The diamond vehicle: the Buddhism of Tibet and the Himalayas, named for what cannot be broken and cuts through.
screen: `VAJRAYANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the diamond vehicle. Today, notice one thing in you that stays steady no matter how the day goes, and one thing the day could use cutting through. Day three hundred five.

screen: `DAY 305 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OM MANI PADME HUM.`

306.title: Om mani padme hum
306.hook: the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara, whom Tibetans call Chenrezig
306.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists recite Om mani padme hum aloud or under their breath through the day, often counting on a string of 108 beads, and carve or paint it on stones placed along paths and on walls that walkers pass on their right-hand side.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vajrayana, and your line, the diamond vehicle. Did you find something steady in you, or something worth cutting through? Day three hundred six.
screen: `VAJRAYANA — THE DIAMOND VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: Walk any path in the Tibetan Himalaya and you'll pass stones with writing carved into them, sometimes painted, sometimes piled into long walls taller than you. Walk past an old woman on a bench in Dharamsala or Kathmandu, and you may hear her murmuring, beads slipping through her fingers, the same short sound again and again. It's the same six syllables on the stones and on her lips. Some people say them tens of thousands of times a day. Today: the most spoken words in Tibet.
screen: `CARVED STONES BY THE PATH.` → `BEADS AND A MURMUR.` → `THE SAME SIX SYLLABLES.`

segments.voice: Om mani padme hum. In Tibetan it's usually said om mani peme hung. It's the mantra of Avalokiteshvara, whom you met in the Heart Sutra, looking deep. Tibetans call him Chenrezig, the one who looks with eyes of compassion, and many regard the Dalai Lama as his living expression. The mantra first appears in an Indian Mahayana text from well over a thousand years ago, and it traveled to Tibet with the teachers. What does it mean? Om is a sacred syllable, older than Buddhism. Mani means jewel. Padme has to do with the lotus. Hum is a seed syllable with no dictionary meaning. So the famous English reading is the jewel in the lotus. That phrase comes from nineteenth-century European scholars, and many scholars now think the grammar points elsewhere, perhaps to a call: O jewel-lotus one. Nobody can settle it for certain. Tibetan teachers tend to explain it by what it does, not by grammar. The jewel is the wish to help others. The lotus, which grows clean out of mud, is wisdom. Together they're the whole path: compassion and wisdom joined. Many teachers also link the six syllables to the six realms of rebirth, as if each syllable eases the suffering of one. And the stones? Carving the mantra, or paying someone to carve it, is an act of merit, and the stones are left where travelers will pass them, keeping them on their right as they walk. The mantra is so short that anyone can carry it. That's much of the point. The jewel in the lotus.
screen: `CHENREZIG — EYES OF COMPASSION.` · `JEWEL, LOTUS, TWO SYLLABLES.` · `THE MEANING IS STILL DEBATED.` · `COMPASSION AND WISDOM JOINED.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL IN THE LOTUS.`

segments.voice: Here's an invitation. If you'd like, say the mantra softly twenty-one times, counting on your fingers, or on beads if you have them: om mani padme hum. Keep it slow and low, more a murmur than a chant. If saying it doesn't feel right for you, simply listen to it inwardly, or just count twenty-one breaths. Either way, when you finish, let the sound fade, and sit in what's left. The bell holds the time.
Om mani padme hum. The six-syllable mantra of Chenrezig, often read as the jewel in the lotus: compassion and wisdom, joined.
screen: `OM MANI PADME HUM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the jewel in the lotus. Today, notice one moment where kindness and clear seeing need each other, and let them work together. Day three hundred six.

307.title: Wheels and flags
307.hook: prayer wheels turned by hand, prayer flags in the wind: the mantra carried by movement
307.tomorrow: Four thoughts that turn the mind
307.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists spin hand-held and monastery prayer wheels clockwise, often while walking around a temple, and hang five-colored prayer flags on passes and rooftops, often renewing them at the Tibetan New Year and retiring faded ones respectfully.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: om mani padme hum, and your line, the jewel in the lotus. Did kindness and clear seeing work together somewhere? Day three hundred seven.
screen: `OM MANI PADME HUM — THE JEWEL IN THE LOTUS.`

segments.voice: A few weeks ago you met a koan: two monks arguing over a flag in the wind. Is the flag moving, or the wind? Today there are more flags. Thousands of them. Strung across mountain passes, from rooftops, over bridges, snapping in colors against the sky. And beside the monastery walls, rows of painted drums on spindles, and pilgrims walking past, spinning each one with the right hand as they go. Nobody's reading anything. And yet, Tibetans say, the words are being said. Today: wheels and flags.
screen: `THE FLAG AND THE WIND, AGAIN.` → `THOUSANDS OF FLAGS ON A PASS.` → `DRUMS SPINNING UNDER HANDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the wheel. Tibetans call it a mani wheel, after yesterday's mantra. Inside the drum is a long, tightly rolled scroll printed with om mani padme hum, over and over, sometimes many thousands of times. Turn the drum once, clockwise, and tradition counts it as saying every mantra inside. There are small wheels held in the hand, with a weight on a chain that keeps them spinning. There are giant wheels in their own little houses. There are wheels set in streams so the water turns them all day and night, and small ones that spin in the rising heat of a lamp. Now the flags. A traditional set has five colors in a fixed order: blue, white, red, green, yellow, often linked to sky, wind, fire, water and earth. Each flag is printed with mantras and prayers, and many carry a horse with a jewel on its back. That's the lungta, the wind horse. The flags aren't hung to send blessings to the person who hung them. They're hung high so the wind carries the blessing outward, to every being it touches. And they're meant to fade. Sun and wind wear the print away, and in a sense that's the mantra going out into the world. New flags are often hung at the Tibetan New Year, and old ones are retired with respect, never tossed on the ground. Does a spinning drum really count? Tibetans answer in different ways. Many trust it simply. Many teachers add that the turning means most when the mind turns with it, toward others. Either way, the teaching gets carried by movement: hands, water, fire, air. The wind carries it.
screen: `A SCROLL ROLLED INSIDE A DRUM.` · `HANDS, WATER, FIRE TURN IT.` · `FIVE COLORS AND THE WIND HORSE.` · `MEANT TO FADE, MEANT FOR ALL.` · then, large: `THE WIND CARRIES IT.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, try moving something mindfully. It could be a cup turned slowly in your hands, or just your hand drawing a slow circle in the air, clockwise. With each turn, send a small wish outward, to no one in particular: may someone somewhere be at ease. Three or four turns is enough. Then set it down, rest your hands, and feel the stillness after the movement. Let the breath do the turning now. The bell holds the time.
Wheels and flags. Prayer wheels turned by hands, water and heat; prayer flags that let the wind carry the mantra out to all beings.
screen: `WHEELS AND FLAGS — today's word`.

308.title: Four thoughts that turn the mind
308.word: Four thoughts that turn the mind
308.hook: precious human life, death, karma, the faults of samsara
308.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often recite and reflect on the four thoughts at the start of each practice session, and they form the first part of the preliminary practices (ngöndro) taught in all the Tibetan schools.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: wheels and flags, and your line, the wind carries it. Did you do one kind thing nobody will credit you for? Day three hundred eight, the end of the week.
screen: `WHEELS AND FLAGS — THE WIND CARRIES IT.`

segments.voice: Most people change direction only after a jolt. A doctor's call. A birthday with a zero on the end. A friend who was fine last month, and isn't. For a week or two, everything looks different: what matters, what doesn't, how you want to spend your hours. Then the feeling fades and the old grooves take over. Tibetan teachers noticed this long ago, and they built the jolt into the very start of the path, on purpose, so it wouldn't depend on bad news. Today: four thoughts that turn the mind.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S CALL. A BIRTHDAY.` → `EVERYTHING LOOKS DIFFERENT.` → `THEN THE OLD GROOVES RETURN.`

segments.voice: In Tibetan practice, these four reflections come before everything else, and people return to them for a lifetime. The first is precious human life. Tibetan teachers borrow an image the Buddha gives in the Pali discourses: a blind turtle in the great ocean rises to the surface once every hundred years, and a wooden yoke with one hole drifts on the waves. The turtle will put its head through that hole, the Buddha says, sooner than a being who has fallen into the lower realms will win back a human birth. So this life, with the time and freedom to learn anything at all, is rare. The second is death and impermanence. Death is certain; its time is not. The third is karma: actions have results, and the small ones add up. The fourth is the faults of samsara, the round of birth and death: even the good parts don't last, and chasing them never quite satisfies. The twelfth-century teacher Gampopa taught all four in a famous book, and the preliminary practices set them in this order, which matters. First you see how lucky you are. Then how short the time is. Then how much your actions count. Then that more chasing won't fix it. Put together, the mind turns, like a boat swinging around in the current, toward the path. Now look back at the week. For a while. The question is still open. Virtue, calm, wisdom. The elders' day. Then the climb: the diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. And today: turn the mind.
screen: `PRECIOUS HUMAN LIFE.` · `DEATH IS CERTAIN, ITS TIME IS NOT.` · `ACTIONS HAVE RESULTS.` · `CHASING NEVER QUITE SATISFIES.` · then, large: `TURN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: For this sit, choose one of the four and stay with it. If you choose precious human life, picture the turtle and the yoke, and then look at your own hands: here you are, with time to sit. If you choose death, rest in the thought that this breath is one of a limited number. Don't push toward a feeling. Just let the thought sit beside you, the way you'd sit beside a friend. When the mind wanders, return to the one you chose. The bell holds the time.
Four thoughts that turn the mind. Precious human life, death, karma, and the faults of samsara: the reflections that start the Tibetan path.
screen: `FOUR THOUGHTS THAT TURN THE MIND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: turn the mind. Today, when the day pulls you into an old groove, pause and ask: given how rare and short this is, what would I choose instead? Day three hundred eight.

fork.setup: you've just heard that human life is precious and death's timing unknown. a Tibetan teacher asks what you'll do with that. which answer fits the four thoughts?
options: panic and try to do everything at once.
let it turn the mind toward what matters, steadily.
forget it; it's too gloomy.
fork.reveal: the four thoughts aren't meant to frighten but to turn the mind, like a boat in the current, toward the path.

original.note: Tibetan blo ldog rnam bzhi: blo (mind) + ldog (turn back) + rnam bzhi (the four): the four thoughts that turn the mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: gloomy thoughts to make you feel bad.
what it means: four reflections that turn the mind toward the path: luck, urgency, care, and seeing through the chase.

what a scholar hears: Gampopa's Jewel Ornament of Liberation teaches all four early on, after buddha-nature; as the 'common' preliminaries of ngöndro they are shared by Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug alike.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 129, Balapandita Sutta (the blind turtle and the yoke)
Gampopa, Jewel Ornament of Liberation (the four thoughts)
